title: Deployment, Fleets & Safety
blurb: Tests defence in depth for physical systems, OTA constraints and canary rollouts, digital twins against training simulators, independent safety monitors, watchdogs and graceful degradation, human-robot safety, and what the safety monitor and canary did and didn't fix.

ideas.title: What the safety layers did and didn't fix

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's organising principle?
options: Always trust the learned policy once it passes testing.
Prefer cloud control so updates can roll back instantly.
Never let one thing be the only barrier against a bad outcome.
Update every device at once to keep the fleet consistent.
questions.explanation: Each technique adds an independent layer to catch what the one before missed.

questions.prompt: Which OTA constraints does a physical fleet have that a cloud service lacks? Select all that apply.
options: Rollback takes time the device may spend doing the wrong thing
A device may be offline and unable to receive it
Updates can't be signed or verified
A device may be mid-task when an update arrives
questions.explanation: The chapter lists mid-task devices, intermittent connectivity and slow rollback. Verifying updates is part of applying them, not an impossibility.

questions.prompt: staged_rollout uses threshold = 0.85. The baseline success rate is 0.922. Below what canary success rate does it halt? Give three decimal places.
questions.explanation: 0.85 × 0.922 = 0.784. The bad update's canary scored 0.542, so it halted.

questions.prompt: What is the trade-off in setting the rollback threshold?
options: Too strict blocks good updates. Too loose lets bad ones in.
Too strict uses more bandwidth. Too loose uses less.
Too strict slows the devices. Too loose speeds them up.
There's no trade-off. Higher thresholds are always safer.
questions.explanation: No setting removes both errors. Choose based on which error costs more for the fleet.

questions.prompt: How does a digital twin differ from a training simulator?
options: It mirrors one real asset, synced to its sensors.
It is a faster training simulator with simpler physics.
They are the same tool under two names.
It is a simulator used only for vision policies.
questions.explanation: Domain randomization covers many realities so policies generalise. A twin's whole point is accuracy to one device.

questions.prompt: Why must a safety monitor not consult the policy's own confidence?
options: Confidence scores are too slow to compute in real time.
Policies don't produce confidence scores.
It would double the monitor's memory use.
A check that trusts what it's checking isn't a check.
questions.explanation: The policy can be confidently wrong out of distribution. The monitor's rule must be independently verifiable.

questions.prompt: What does a watchdog timer do?
options: Measures how long the policy takes to train.
Logs every action for later audit.
Falls back safely if the loop goes quiet.
Counts how many updates a device has received.
questions.explanation: Missing a heartbeat means something failed, so the system falls back rather than acting on stale or absent decisions.

questions.prompt: A camera fails mid-task. What does graceful degradation call for?
options: A defined, safe reduced-capability mode
Retraining the policy on the spot
Shutting down the whole fleet
Continuing on the last good frame indefinitely
questions.explanation: The system shouldn't silently run on bad or missing input. It should drop to a known safe mode.

questions.prompt: What extra safety dimension appears when robots share space with people?
options: Bandwidth, so commands reach the robot faster
Accuracy, so the policy never makes mistakes
Storage, so every interaction is recorded
Legibility, so people can predict its motion
questions.explanation: Collision-free by an internal metric isn't enough. Speed and separation monitoring and clear emergency stops are standard.

questions.prompt: How does the chapter treat standards like ISO 10218 and ISO/TS 15066?
options: As optional extras for large fleets only
As evidence standards exist, not as guidance
As outdated rules that no longer apply
As a complete checklist that guarantees compliance
questions.explanation: The chapter says to consult current, domain-specific, qualified regulatory expertise before deploying.

questions.prompt: The safety monitor cut collisions from 11/40 to 0/40. What happened to task success?
options: It stayed at 0/40. Only the damage was bounded.
It fell, since the monitor blocked useful actions.
It rose to 11/40, matching the collisions avoided.
It rose to 40/40, since collisions no longer interrupted runs.
questions.explanation: Safety layers aren't fixes. The policy still needs DAgger-style correction.

questions.prompt: The bad update reached 10 devices with a canary instead of all 200. By what factor did that cut the blast radius?
questions.explanation: 200 / 10 = 20. The update was just as bad wherever it landed, about 0.54–0.55 success.

questions.prompt: A team ships a robot whose cloned policy fails off-distribution, protected by a safety monitor, and closes the policy ticket. What does the chapter say?
options: That's fine. Zero collisions means the problem is solved.
That's a mistake, because monitors make policies worse.
That's fine, as long as the canary rollout passed too.
That's a mistake. Safe failures still need fixing.
questions.explanation: The trade-offs section warns against calling the capability gap solved because a safety net exists. Defence in depth bounds damage, it doesn't fix the cause.

bookExercises.prompt: State this chapter's organising principle ("defense in depth") in one sentence, and explain why a safety monitor consulting the policy's own confidence score would violate it.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Never let one thing be the only thing standing between a decision and a bad outcome. Every safeguard should be an independent layer that can catch what the layer before it missed. A safety monitor consulting the policy's own confidence score would violate this because it would no longer be independent. A policy that fails confidently (exactly the failure mode this chapter names) would report high confidence on its own wrong decision, and a monitor trusting that confidence score would fail to catch exactly the case it exists to catch.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain the difference between a training simulator and a digital twin in one or two sentences, and state which one domain randomization applies to.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A training simulator deliberately covers a distribution of possible realities (via domain randomization) so a trained policy generalises; a digital twin is a virtual replica of one specific real asset, kept in sync with that asset's actual sensor data, for monitoring and diagnosing that exact device. Domain randomization applies to the training simulator, not the digital twin. Accuracy to one specific reality is the digital twin's entire point, the opposite of domain randomization's goal.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's safety-monitor results (11/40 collisions without, 0/40 with, task success 0/40 in both), explain why reporting only the collision numbers without also reporting the unchanged task-success rate would risk a misleading impression of what the safety monitor accomplished.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Reporting only "collisions dropped from 11/40 to 0/40" without also noting task success stayed at 0/40 in both conditions risks the misleading impression that the safety monitor "fixed" the robot or made it more capable, when in fact the underlying policy is exactly as bad at the task as before; the monitor only prevented that badness from producing collisions. Reporting both numbers together makes clear that a safety layer bounds damage without improving capability, which is precisely this chapter's central distinction between "fixing the problem" and "bounding the damage while the problem gets fixed properly."

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's rollout comparison (staged: 10/200 devices exposed to the bad update; all-at-once: 200/200), compute the blast-radius reduction factor, and explain what specifically about Scenario B's canary success rate (0.542 vs. 0.922 baseline) triggered the halt before the full fleet was exposed.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `200 / 10 = 20x` blast-radius reduction. Scenario B's canary success rate (0.542) fell well below the threshold-adjusted baseline expectation (0.85 × 0.922 ≈ 0.784), triggering `staged_rollout`'s halt condition. The canary group's measured performance was low enough, relative to the pre-update baseline, to signal a real regression rather than normal variation, which is exactly the evidence needed to stop the rollout before the remaining 190 devices received the same bad update.

bookExercises.prompt: A team ships a robot with a safety monitor that successfully eliminates all collisions in testing, and considers the project's safety work complete. Using this chapter's Trade-offs section and Worked Example, write the two or three sentences you'd say before agreeing.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "This chapter's own Worked Example shows exactly why that's premature: the safety monitor eliminated all collisions, but the underlying policy's task-success rate stayed at 0/40, completely unchanged. A safety net bounds damage; it doesn't fix the capability gap that made the dangerous behavior possible in the first place. The actual policy work (better or more demonstrations, a DAgger-style fix) is still an open problem, and calling the project 'safety complete' risks shipping a robot that safely fails at its job forever rather than fixing why it fails."

bookExercises.prompt: Procedure 65.2's rollback threshold is a tunable parameter. Describe a concrete fleet scenario where setting the threshold too strict (blocking updates too easily) would itself become a real operational cost, not just a minor inconvenience.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A fleet running frequent, low-risk software updates (e.g. minor logging or telemetry improvements) with a rollback threshold set too strictly could see legitimately good updates repeatedly blocked by normal performance variance across the canary group. Each blocked update requires manual investigation and re-deployment, consuming engineering time and delaying genuinely beneficial fixes (security patches, bug fixes) from ever reaching the fleet, which is a real operational cost even though no dangerous update was ever actually deployed.

bookExercises.prompt: Read about ISO/TS 15066's Speed and Separation Monitoring (SSM) requirement for collaborative robots. Explain in your own words why SSM's requirement, that a robot's speed must decrease as a human gets closer, is a form of defense in depth distinct from a simple emergency-stop button.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Speed and Separation Monitoring requires a robot to continuously reduce its speed as a human approaches, rather than operating at full speed until a hard boundary is crossed and then stopping abruptly. This is a distinct, additional layer from an emergency-stop button because it acts proactively and continuously (reducing risk exposure well before any critical threshold is reached) rather than reactively and only at one hard boundary. If the continuous speed-reduction layer fails or is insufficient, the emergency-stop remains as a separate, independent final layer, exactly the defense-in-depth principle from this chapter's Motivation: multiple independent layers, each catching what the layer before it might miss, rather than relying on a single hard-stop mechanism as the only safeguard.
